source.title: Sloth: scaling laws for LLM skills to predict multi-benchmark performance across families
source.authors: F. Polo; Seamus Somerstep; Leshem Choshen; Yue-Kai Sun; Mikhail Yurochkin

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream-performance predictability using benchmark scores and latent skills rather than the original held-out cross-entropy loss measurement.
record.gate_note: The study's leaderboard cross-validation and downstream-task predictions bear on V6. The paper also reports skill-maximising compute allocations, but these optimise latent skills rather than held-out loss; they are recorded under fits_no_version. No cross-entropy loss scaling results are reported.
record.test_reason: Fits benchmark-score scaling laws (size, tokens, family intercepts, latent skills) on public leaderboard data. It predicts held-out larger models' benchmark, downstream-task and pass@k scores, which bears on V6. It reports no held-out pretraining loss, so V1–V5 are untested. V7 concerns loss exponents and loss-optimal splits, so it is also untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also motivate the work by arguing that a single family-independent benchmark scaling law generalises poorly across model families. Sloth's family-specific efficiency intercepts, estimated from one model per family, fix this. They also report a MAPE version and the shared-intercept variant as qualitatively similar or competitive on some benchmarks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses existing leaderboard scores across model families to fit latent-skill benchmark scaling laws and predict downstream scores; it does not train pretraining runs and fit held-out cross-entropy power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction and curve shape vary with the scaling model and fitting choices, including trainable versus fixed sigmoid link functions, family-specific intercepts, and PCA+FLOPs versus Sloth; model-family data availability also affects setup.

fits_no_version.finding: The skill-maximising allocation under 6st=c differs by skill. Reasoning favours parameters (72B at 0.45T tokens for 1.9e23 FLOPs). Knowledge and instruction following favour tokens (2.15B at 15T), bounded by the data support.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal allocations for benchmark-derived latent skills differ by skill and from loss-optimal rules.

record.problems: The paper reports no error bars or statistical significance for the main prediction results. Several downstream predictions and curve comparisons are presented in figures without extractable numeric values. The authors note that prediction usually depends on data from at least one model in the target family and that flexible learned links lack guarantees for extrapolation to very different models.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no loss is reported.
Extrapolation of loss power laws to much larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token split; the paper only optimises latent skills (see fits_no_version).
Depth, width and architecture effects at fixed parameter count.
Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss exponents and the compute-optimal split on fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-benchmark and per-family MAE showing large errors for some benchmarks and families. Examples: FLOPs shared-intercept GSM8K 12.4 pp on v1; some family averages exceed 10–30 pp. This shows uneven predictability.
A second setting with two test-family models observed, giving family-specific slopes. It also has absolute MAE values (e.g. FLOPs v1 average 9.4 pp).

record.verdict_notes: All evidence concerns benchmark scores and observational leaderboard data; no models are trained and no loss is measured. Rows r1 and r2 compare the study's own method with baselines; only their absolute MAEs bear on V6. No error bars are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fit on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs' held-out loss.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute; the paper instead optimises latent skills.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Does not test downstream prediction from pretraining loss itself; coverage is benchmark-score and latent-skill-based prediction in the reported settings.
Tests fitting and curve-shape dependence for downstream benchmark scores, not cross-entropy exponents or loss-optimal compute allocation.

source_check.notes: The supplied source is arXiv v5 dated 1 December 2025. The authors acknowledge dependence on target-family observations and no extrapolation guarantee for models very different from the training population.

statements.correction: Figure 1; smallest target-family model observed; Sloth d=3 average MAE: leaderboard v1 4.2 percentage points, leaderboard v2 3.5 percentage points; family-specific FLOPs baseline: v1 4.4 percentage points.
statements.problem: The qualitative conclusion and small-family-member calibration condition are supported. However, 3.5–4.4 percentage points is not a correctly identified Sloth average range: Figure 1's v1 value 4.4 belongs to the FLOPs baseline.

statements.correction: Figure 1, leaderboard v1 average MAE: FLOPs with shared intercept 7.8 percentage points; FLOPs with family-specific intercept 4.4; Sloth d=3 with family-specific intercepts 4.2. Section 4.2 and Figure 3: shared-intercept Sloth competitive on some benchmarks. V6 verdict for these mixed conditions: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The numbers exist, but 7.8 versus 4.2 compares shared-intercept FLOPs with Sloth d=3, rather than isolating an intercept change. Shared-intercept Sloth can perform competitively on some benchmarks. These mixed results warrant limits_scope rather than an unqualified challenges characterization.

statements.correction: Figure 1, leaderboard v1 average MAE: shared-intercept FLOPs 7.8 percentage points; family-specific-intercept FLOPs 4.4; family-specific-intercept Sloth d=3 4.2. Test-family calibration uses its smallest model.
statements.problem: The reported pair changes the model formulation as well as family intercepts, so it cannot establish that Sloth's MAE changes from 7.8 to 4.2 solely through intercept calibration.
